690.bp: When scientists study human behavior using online data — tweets, clicks, survey responses — they need everyone to trust and understand how they got their answers. Right now, researchers often can't easily share their exact steps or let others repeat the work, which means we can't be sure the findings are real.
690.wh: The core tension is that social science lives in a world of messy, constantly-changing platforms and privacy rules, while computer science demands precise, reproducible steps. A researcher's workflow lives on platforms (Twitter, Instagram) that change their rules, hide their data, or vanish; the researcher uses custom scripts that nobody else can run. There's no agreement on what 'reproducible' even means here.
690.ap: R2CASS is a workshop that brings together social scientists, computer people, and policy makers to agree on shared tools and checklists. They've built Methods Hub, a platform where researchers post their workflows step-by-step, share templates for common tasks, and check each other's work. The workshop runs hands-on sessions where people actually try to repeat one another's computational social science projects.
690.ww: When researchers can see exactly what someone else did — their data sources, their code, their judgment calls — they can spot where things break down and fix them. Publishing the steps also forces researchers to be clearer about what they're assuming, which makes the science stronger. Templates and shared checklists make it easy to follow best practices without having to reinvent the wheel.
690.po: The payoff is that computational social science research becomes credible enough to guide real decisions. A policymaker can look at a study and actually verify it's sound. The Methods Hub platform lowers the barrier: a researcher can now run a reproducible task on the platform and get feedback in real time, making the whole field more transparent and trustworthy.

691.bp: Large language models power many web services — chatbots, search, recommendations — and companies want to adapt these giant models to work better for their specific needs without sharing their users' private data. Federated learning lets teams collaborate on training without handing over sensitive information.
691.wh: The catch is that different teams have different privacy budgets: some users tolerate almost no noise, others accept heavy privacy protection. When you average together updates from clients with wildly different privacy levels, the noisy updates corrupt the good ones, dragging down overall performance. Meanwhile, clients with strong privacy demands get punished — their data helps everyone, but they see worse results.
691.ap: WinFLoRA uses a clever carrot-and-stick approach: it estimates how much privacy noise each client added to their updates, then gives more influence to the clients who added less noise. Think of it as weighting votes — a clean update from one client counts for more than a noisy one. The system automatically learns which clients are trustworthy and shapes the final model to reflect their updates more heavily.
691.ww: This works because it aligns incentives. A client who cares less about privacy and contributes clean updates sees their preferences reflected in the shared model, improving their own task performance. A client with strict privacy needs gets protected without being punished — their updates still matter, just proportionally to their noise level. The system finds the sweet spot where everyone's interests balance.
691.po: Experiments show WinFLoRA achieves up to 52% higher accuracy and up to 2.56x better utility for individual clients compared to simpler baselines. Clients now have a reason to be honest about their privacy needs and to contribute better data, because the system rewards them for it. This makes federated learning actually work in the real messy world where privacy policies clash.

692.bp: On e-commerce sites, customers don't just click once and disappear — they click on an item, favorite it, add it to cart, and maybe buy it. Understanding this sequence of different actions is the key to knowing what they really want so recommendations can be both accurate and fast at scale.
692.wh: Traditional methods treat all behavior types the same or try to predict one at a time, missing the fact that watching someone favorite then cart an item tells you something different than watching them favorite then abandon. Most prior work uses transformer-based models that can learn these patterns perfectly but are glacially slow on long sequences — they compute pairwise relationships between every action, which becomes impossible on real shopping carts with hundreds of actions.
692.ap: TGA (Transition-Aware Graph Attention Network) recognizes that not all behavior pairs matter equally and builds a sparse, structured graph that only keeps the transitions that actually teach you something. It identifies which transitions are informative from three angles: do items themselves predict the next action, do product categories, and do the user's recent neighbors in the graph. Then it runs a fast, lightweight attention mechanism on just that sparse graph instead of the dense pairwise matrix.
692.ww: This works because real shopping behavior is structured, not random. Certain transitions repeat — people who favorite often go to cart; people who buy rarely go back to favoriting — and the algorithm learns to focus on those patterns. By ignoring noisy transitions and focusing on the few that carry information, you keep the model accurate while cutting computation time from polynomial (slow) to linear (fast).
692.po: The payoff is that recommendation engines can handle long shopping sequences in real time without becoming a bottleneck. Industrial e-commerce platforms with millions of users can now use sophisticated behavior-aware recommendations instead of settling for simpler, faster approximations. Experiments show better accuracy while keeping latency low enough for live serving.

693.bp: Real recommendation systems don't just maximize accuracy — they have hard business rules: every recommendation list must have items from multiple sellers, must include at least one new product, must be diverse enough to appeal to different tastes. These aren't polite suggestions; breaking them even once breaks customer trust and violates partnerships.
693.wh: Most machine learning models treat rules as soft penalties — a gentle push toward fairness or coverage. But in production, a single constraint violation is a failure. Meanwhile, multi-objective optimization (balancing accuracy, fairness, diversity) requires exploring many trade-offs, and large language models are good at talking about tradeoffs but not at guaranteeing hard constraints are met.
693.ap: DualAgent-Rec splits the problem into two specialized agents: one focuses solely on ranking items accurately while respecting hard constraints (using classical algorithms proven to enforce rules), the other explores diverse combinations without constraints (searching the Pareto frontier — the space where you can't improve one goal without hurting another). An LLM-based coordinator watches progress and adaptively shifts resources between the agents, asking the constrained agent to do more work when constraints are in danger of breaking, and letting the exploration agent push for diversity when room exists.
693.ww: This works because it separates concerns: the constrained agent brings mathematical guarantees about feasibility, the exploration agent brings creativity and diversity, and the LLM coordinator brings judgment about when to trust which. By using an LLM as the orchestrator rather than the optimizer, you get flexibility without sacrificing the hard mathematical guarantees that safety-critical systems need.
693.po: Experiments on real Amazon shopping data show 100% constraint satisfaction across all test cases while improving overall quality (measured by Pareto hypervolume) by 4–6% over existing methods. This is the difference between a system that occasionally violates seller agreements and one that never does, while still giving customers better recommendations.

694.bp: PFAS chemicals — forever chemicals that don't break down in the environment and persist in drinking water and wildlife — need to be tracked, studied, and regulated. Scientists, regulators, and companies need a shared, structured vocabulary for talking about which PFAS molecules are which, their properties, and what we know about their environmental impact.
694.wh: The challenge is that chemical data is scattered across different databases using different naming schemes, properties are measured under different conditions, and toxicology information is buried in research papers. A regulator trying to understand what PFAS are in drinking water in one region can't easily connect that to research from another country or to EPA toxicity data because nobody standardized the language.
694.ap: The CompTox ontology is a structured dictionary that hierarchically organizes PFAS — types include fluorotelomers and perfluoroalkyl acids, each with detailed properties like molecular mass, carbon chain length, and functional groups. Each chemical gets authoritative identifiers (like DTXSID numbers), properties (chemical fingerprints), and links to environmental and toxicological data. The ontology is built using a template-driven process and formatted in OWL, a language computers can understand and reason about.
694.ww: When information is structured this way, scientists and regulators can now ask precise questions: 'Show me all perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids with chain length greater than 6 that have high bioaccumulation potential.' Computers can automatically link data from different sources by matching identifiers and properties. Research papers mentioning PFAS can be automatically catalogued. This transforms scattered knowledge into a queryable, reasoned system.
694.po: The ontology enables integrated PFAS monitoring and risk assessment at scale. A water utility testing for contamination can query which PFAS are highest risk, what properties predict environmental persistence, and how monitored levels compare to regulatory data. Scientists studying one PFAS can discover related ones. The structured representation makes it possible to govern PFAS informed by complete data instead of isolated anecdotes.

695.bp: The cryptography that protects your banking, email, and web browsing — RSA encryption — works because factoring huge numbers is mathematically hard. But quantum computers could break this in years, threatening all the security we built over decades. Understanding exactly how quantum algorithms would attack RSA helps us prepare.
695.wh: Quantum computing is abstract and hard to visualize; most people can't follow quantum gate operations or understand why Shor's algorithm breaks RSA. Existing explanations either oversimplify to the point of being wrong or get so technical that only specialists can follow. We need a clear, traceable explanation that shows exactly how quantum processes would extract RSA's secret.
695.ap: This paper builds a quantum emulator using dictionaries: each quantum state is stored as dictionary[bitstring] = complex_number, where the complex number represents the quantum amplitude at that state. Each quantum gate is implemented as a rule: the Hadamard gate creates superposition by duplicating dictionary keys; phase gates rotate amplitudes; X and Toffoli gates flip bits conditionally. By stepping through these rules, you can watch a quantum computer search for the period of a number, which reveals the RSA factors.
695.ww: This approach works because dictionary-based simulation stays concrete and traceable — you can see exactly which bitstrings matter at each step and why. It reveals that quantum advantage comes from superposition (the dictionary holding many states at once) and interference (amplitudes cancelling or adding up). By making the quantum process visible, the paper shows why quantum computers have a path to RSA that classical computers don't.
695.po: The payoff is understanding: this framework makes the quantum threat to RSA not abstract but mechanical and viewable. Security teams can now grasp why RSA will eventually need replacement, researchers can teach quantum computing in a more grounded way, and anyone curious can follow the logic. The paper doesn't prevent the threat, but it demystifies it so we can prepare seriously.

696.bp: Researchers increasingly use large language models to simulate how different people with different backgrounds would answer surveys — instead of paying hundreds of respondents, they prompt an LLM with a persona and generate synthetic responses. This is cheap and fast, but does it actually capture real diversity?
696.wh: The intuition is that adding persona details (age, education, income, political leaning) to an LLM prompt should make it roleplay better and thus answer surveys more like real people. But LLMs are language patterns, not human simulators — they might distort certain beliefs, miss nuanced attitudes, or respond differently to demographic cues than real people do. The real question: does persona prompting reduce or increase error?
696.ap: The paper tests this against a large real-world survey dataset (World Values Survey with 70K respondent-question pairs). They prompt two open LLMs with and without persona details, asking them to answer each question as a simulated respondent. Then they compare: does the LLM's simulated answer match the real person's answer? They measure both aggregate alignment and subgroup-specific accuracy.
696.ww: The finding is uncomfortable: persona prompting doesn't reliably improve performance and in many cases makes it worse. The effect is highly heterogeneous — most questions stay the same, but some questions and underrepresented groups see large distortions. For example, an LLM might overfit to stereotype a persona, answering political questions in a caricature rather than the nuanced way real people do.
696.po: The payoff is a warning: researchers using LLMs to simulate respondents are not just approximating; they're potentially redistributing error in ways that hide minority perspectives. A study claiming to represent a 65-year-old woman from rural areas might be simulating a media stereotype instead. This suggests either dropping the persona-based simulation approach or validating heavily against real data before trusting the results.

697.bp: Cities generate vast amounts of data — sensor networks tracking traffic, air quality, energy use, crime. But most cities collect this data, analyze it separately, and then don't actually act on it. The gap between 'we know there will be congestion in 2 hours' and 'traffic lights already adapted' is where real impact dies.
697.wh: Predictive models often exist in isolation from operations. A traffic prediction system can't automatically adjust signal timing; the prediction sits in a dashboard waiting for a human to notice and act. Meanwhile, the model never learns whether the prediction was accurate or helpful. This breaks the feedback loop that makes AI systems get better — and it wastes the opportunity to prevent problems before they happen.
697.ap: This paper proposes a closed-loop architecture that connects four pieces: sensors feed data to AI/ML models, predictions feed to decision-support dashboards, decisions trigger real-world actions (changing signal timing, rerouting buses, activating resources), and outcomes flow back to retrain and refine the models. The architecture includes 'digital twins' — virtual simulations of the city — that help test decisions before deployment.
697.ww: This works because feedback is the engine of improvement. When a traffic prediction triggers an action and you measure the outcome, the model learns what worked and what didn't. This transforms prediction from hindsight to foresight — instead of explaining what happened, the system prevents it. Also, by closing the loop, you catch errors quickly: if a prediction is wrong and nobody acts on it, the model course-corrects for next time.
697.po: Cities can shift from reactive (responding to congestion after it happens) to preventive (stopping congestion before it starts). Response times to emergencies drop because signals, resources, and personnel are already positioned. Over time, the models get better because they learn from real outcomes. The payoff is smoother traffic, faster emergency response, and more resilient cities.

698.bp: Real online shopping has a long tail: most customers buy popular items, but the profit often comes from selling niche products to the right people. Recommending these hidden gems is hard because they have few interactions for the algorithm to learn from. If an algorithm can't find patterns in data, it fails.
698.wh: Collaborative filtering — learning from 'people like you bought this' — works great for popular items with lots of interaction data. But for long-tail items with maybe three purchases ever, there's simply not enough data to detect patterns. Meanwhile, large language models can read product descriptions and understand that two semantically similar niche items go together, but LLM semantics live in a different space from collaborative patterns, and it's unclear how to combine them without one drowning out the other.
698.ap: FCRLLM uses a 'flipped classroom' dynamic: normally a teacher (LLM) teaches students (collaborative model). Here, the framework flips it — the collaborative model's attention patterns actively shape what the LLM focuses on, pulling semantic understanding toward real user interactions. The mechanism uses energy-based learning (inspired by neural networks that find stable states) so that collaborative and semantic signals pull toward a common representation instead of fighting.
698.ww: This works because both signals are right but incompatible on first glance: collaborative filtering sees 'these users interact' while LLM semantics sees 'these items are conceptually close.' By letting them negotiate via energy minimization, the model finds representations where both constraints hold — semantic neighbor items end up close in the space when collaborative data supports it, but only then.
698.po: Experiments show the method works on real shopping datasets with long-tail items. Niche products now get recommended to the right customers more often, driving revenue from items that would otherwise languish. The collaborative signal grounds LLM semantics in real user behavior, avoiding over-generalization, while the LLM signal compensates for cold-start problems on unpopular items.

699.bp: Misinformation spreads fast online: a photo of a politician from 2010 captioned as 'today' misleads millions before fact-checkers can respond. Out-of-context image-text mismatches — the image and text don't actually belong together — are a major class of misinformation that's hard to detect.
699.wh: Detecting mismatches requires understanding both the image content and the text and reasoning about whether they align. Most approaches either look only at images or only at text, missing the cross-modal contradiction. Methods that use both modalities often rely on external web search to verify claims, which is slow, expensive, and won't work in regions without good search infrastructure. Lightweight methods that work without external data tend to miss subtle mismatches.
699.ap: This framework combines three pieces without needing web evidence: extract semantic entities from the image using object detection, generate a description of what's actually in the image, and combine that description with the text caption into a prompt for a language model (Flan-T5) to judge alignment. In parallel, run a CLIP model that directly assesses image-text visual-semantic match. Then ensemble the two judgments using weights optimized specifically for detecting misinformation.
699.ww: This works because generating descriptions forces the system to commit to what's actually visible, and then asking a language model 'does this description match the text?' catches when text makes a claim the image doesn't support. CLIP independently checks if the image and text 'feel' related semantically. Combining both catches different failure modes: text might claim something false, or text might claim something that could be true but isn't what the image shows.
699.po: The method reaches state-of-the-art accuracy among approaches that don't use external web data, while running fast enough for real-time deployment. A news platform or social network can now flag out-of-context images as users upload them, with modest computational cost. This matters in regions where external verification services are unavailable and where the spread of misinformation is fastest.

700.bp: When computer systems make decisions about people — credit scores, job applications, content moderation — they should treat everyone fairly. But social networks and demographic data are often incomplete: you might know someone's age but not their race, or vice versa. Many fairness solutions invent the missing data, which can introduce new biases.
700.wh: The temptation to fill in missing demographic data is strong — more information seems better. But inventing data guesses about protected characteristics (race, gender, religion) inevitably encodes societal stereotypes and can make fairness worse, not better. Meanwhile, if you ignore the missing data entirely, the model might treat people unfairly simply by accident. The real challenge: how do you ensure fairness without fabricating protected information?
700.ap: FairGE (Fair Graph Encoding) uses spectral graph theory — a mathematical way to understand network structure — instead of generating missing data. It leverages the network's principal eigenvector (the dominant pattern of connections) to capture structural information about each person, then pads the missing demographic attributes with zeros rather than guessing. This mathematical abstraction preserves the network's fairness properties without inventing sensitive data.
700.ww: This works because spectral properties of graphs encode meaningful structural patterns without requiring protected attributes. The principal eigenvector identifies high-influence nodes and structural roles automatically. By using zeros for missing demographics, the system avoids encoding false assumptions. Theoretically, this suppresses biased spectral components while preserving fair ones.
700.po: Experiments on real social networks show at least 16% improvement in both statistical parity (everyone has similar outcome rates) and equality of opportunity (disparities are minimized) compared to methods that generate missing data. Most importantly, fairness improves without requiring invasive demographic data collection, protecting user privacy while making the system more equitable.

701.bp: Vietnamese medicinal plants are a source of traditional knowledge and potential new medicines, but that knowledge is scattered across Vietnamese sources, with names and classifications that don't match global scientific databases. A researcher in Vietnam can't easily search the global biodiversity network using Vietnamese plant names.
701.wh: Biodiversity platforms like GBIF are powerful but English-centric: species are named in Latin and English, the search interface is English-only, and connections to local knowledge are sparse. For Vietnamese researchers, this means starting every search by translating local names to Latin names to use the global system, which is tedious and discourages engagement. Meanwhile, if Vietnamese medicinal plants aren't in global datasets, global conservation and medical research miss potentially important species.
701.ap: Viet Medi Species 2026 assembles 310K images of 4,799 medicinal plant species from Vietnam, using both scientific names (linked to GBIF) and Vietnamese vernacular names. The pipeline automatically extracted and validated images at scale using a reproducible, asynchronous process. The dataset includes metadata tied to Vietnamese culture and knowledge while maintaining links to global taxonomy via GBIF identifiers.
701.ww: This works because it creates a bridge: a Vietnamese person can now search in Vietnamese, find images of medicinal plants they recognize, and automatically discover the global scientific information and research connected to those plants through GBIF. Conversely, a global researcher studying a particular plant family can see how that family appears in Vietnamese traditional medicine.
701.po: Researchers in Vietnam now have a local-language resource for biodiversity that doesn't compromise global integration. The dataset enables new research connecting Vietnamese traditional medicine to modern pharmacology. Most broadly, the project demonstrates a template for including non-English languages and local knowledge in global datasets, enabling more equitable participation in global science.

702.bp: When handed a new dataset you've never seen before — say, a pile of customer service complaints with no categories — how do you systematically figure out what patterns exist? Even with an LLM suggesting rough categories, it's hard to evolve those guesses into a clean, consistent taxonomy.
702.wh: The intuition is that LLMs can generate category suggestions, but rough suggestions aren't enough. You need to step back and see where categories cluster across the full dataset (a 'wide view'), then zoom in and check whether your extraction method consistently identifies those categories (a 'sharp focus'). Most discovery tools do one or the other — either showing you the big picture or validating details — but not both together.
702.ap: Pattern Insights Explorer alternates between two perspectives: wide-lens analysis zooms out and shows which patterns cluster across the full dataset landscape, revealing where meaningful categories emerge. Then sharp-focus validation zooms in on specific examples to verify the extraction method actually works — does it consistently capture the pattern it claims to? The framework refines the taxonomy iteratively, evolving rough sketches into precise categories without needing external ground truth.
702.ww: This works because discovery is naturally rhythmic: you first need to see the big picture (where are patterns hiding?), then zoom in to validate (am I actually finding what I think?). This rhythm prevents two common failures: discovering phantom patterns that don't really exist (you zoom in and find the method isn't reliable), or missing patterns that only show up in certain data regions (you zoomed too far in).
702.po: A team can now take an unfamiliar dataset and systematically extract a clean taxonomy without experts manually labeling everything. The wide-lens and sharp-focus cycle prevents both over-generalization and missed nuances. This is especially valuable for exploratory research where the categories aren't known upfront, and for applied settings where standardizing unstructured data is bottleneck.

703.bp: In social networks with positive and negative relationships — collaborators and rivals, allies and enemies — machine learning models need to predict whether a future connection will be positive or negative. But when an AI model makes a prediction, users need to understand why: what made it think two people should be enemies?
703.wh: Explaining graph neural network predictions is already hard (they integrate information across many steps of neighbors and connections), but signed graphs add a twist: the sign of each relationship matters. Existing explanation methods either ignore signs entirely or return disconnected graph fragments that don't make intuitive sense. A human looking at an explanation needs to see: 'these people are connected through a positive path to you, and a negative path to them, so they should conflict.'
703.ap: SGExplainer uses 'balanced paths' from signed graph theory as its core concept: a balanced path is a sequence of relationships that has internal logic (positive times positive equals positive, positive times negative equals negative, like multiplying numbers). The algorithm learns which nodes and edges to keep by training a mask — a binary layer that highlights subgraph regions — then enforces the constraint that the highlighted subgraph consists of balanced paths. This ensures explanations are both faithful and human-intelligible.
703.ww: This works because balanced paths have intuitive appeal: you can trace a path on a graph, count the signs along the way, and see whether the final result makes sense. This is something a human can verify by hand. By building explanations from balanced paths, the system automatically produces explanations that are both theoretically grounded (faithful to the model's reasoning) and psychologically clear (people understand them).
703.po: The framework generates explanations for link sign predictions that are both accurate and interpretable. A social network platform can now show users: 'we think you and this person will clash because you're both close friends with this mutual friend, but you have opposite opinions, which creates tension.' Experiments show SGExplainer outperforms baseline methods in both explanation quality and efficiency, making real-time interpretability feasible.

704.bp: In e-commerce recommendation systems, feature selection is critical: engineers manually pick which product attributes (color, brand, price, seller) to feed to the recommendation model. Picking the right subset cuts computation while keeping accuracy high. But modern deep learning makes it hard to know which features actually matter.
704.wh: Deep neural networks learn hierarchically: early layers capture low-level features, middle layers combine them, later layers make final decisions. A simple approach asks 'which features matter to the final output?' but this misses layers in the middle where real learning happens. Existing methods estimate feature importance from sensitivity (how much does output change if we perturb this feature?) or from learned gates, but they often rely on just one layer or one batch of samples, making estimates unstable and biased.
704.ap: FairFS identifies three specific bias problems: layer bias (importance estimates depend on which layer you look at), baseline bias (the reference point for what 'no feature' means matters a lot), and approximation bias (how you aggregate signals across samples affects which features look important). FairFS regularizes feature importance across all layers simultaneously, uses a smooth baseline feature close to the classifier's decision boundary, and aggregates approximations carefully to counterbalance these biases.
704.ww: This works because it directly targets the sources of error rather than hoping a single measurement will be right. By demanding consistency across layers, you force the model to agree with itself — if a feature matters early, it should still matter later. A carefully-chosen baseline gives you a sensible 'what does zero information look like?' reference point. Aggregation methods that account for approximation error prevent one noisy sample from dominating.
704.po: The result is more accurate feature importance estimates that recommendation teams can trust to guide their feature selection decisions. This means faster models (fewer features to compute) without sacrificing accuracy. On real industrial systems with thousands of candidate features and millions of users, picking the right 50 features instead of the wrong 50 can save massive computational cost while maintaining recommendation quality.
